implementation_notes: The runtime supplies the endpoint: spawn a task that owns the Receiver and loops on rx.recv().await, calling the service and sending the reply; the channel is runtime-owned, the task is notified when a message arrives, and the bounded variant provides backpressure. The loop ends when recv() returns None, which is the idiomatic shutdown signal once every Sender has been dropped. A hand-rolled registry of boxed handler traits is still justified when the service must be selected dynamically per message.
pitfalls: An unawaited JoinHandle hides a panic: the worker task dies, the activator stops consuming and senders queue or block with no error at the activator.
Leaking one Sender clone keeps recv() from ever returning None, so the worker never shuts down.
UnboundedSender removes backpressure; a service slower than its producers grows the queue without limit - prefer the bounded channel.

variants.name: std::thread worker on std::sync::mpsc (no async runtime)
variants.implementation_notes: Without an async runtime the same endpoint is an OS thread blocked on std::sync::mpsc::Receiver::recv, with sync_channel supplying the bound; recv() returns Err once every Sender is dropped, which ends the loop. This is the form for synchronous services and for crates that must not pull in an async runtime; prefer the tokio form once either the service or the transport is asynchronous.
pitfalls: std::sync::mpsc has no async integration: calling recv() from an async executor thread blocks the whole executor.
A panicking service unwinds the worker thread while producers keep succeeding, so messages accumulate unconsumed; join the handle or supervise the worker.
